# CHAPTER 251

## THE UNDERSTUDY

I learned thirty-eight of the Uncle's forty-three lines before sleep.

This was either excellent or terrible depending on which five remained.

Lyssa woke me by moving around the room quietly enough that I noticed only after she had already dressed.

The pages were beside my hand.

I had apparently gone to sleep with one finger holding my place.

Useful technique if I wanted to learn lines through skin.

I sat up.

My neck objected.

"Morning," Lyssa said.

"Debatable."

She had the darker spool in her work bag now. The reddish-brown sample was still gone. Brown cloth, three pins. Damaged shirt, three threads.

I checked my body because that remained a thing bodies required.

Right shoulder stiff from sleeping badly, not injured. Hands fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb fine. No headache. No mana-related anything.

Five lines.

I picked up the pages.

Lyssa looked at me.

"Food first."

"I know five lines badly."

"Food."

"Possibly six."

She put bread in front of me.

I ate while reading.

This produced neither good eating nor good reading.

The first missing line was in scene one and began with, "A table is an agreement."

I knew the rest after that.

The second was an answer to Hara.

The third was not actually missing. I had combined it with the next line because Pell always paused between them and apparently my memory had stored his pause as punctuation.

That left three.

Lyssa took the page out of my hand.

"Hey."

"Say them."

"What?"

"Without paper."

I stared at her.

She waited.

Fine.

I started at the beginning.

Not performing.

Just words.

The first seven came easily.

Eight arrived late.

Nine through fourteen held.

At fifteen I stopped.

Lyssa looked at the page.

"You have mistaken silence for agreement."

"That's Hara's line."

"Then answer it."

I did.

She continued reading the other parts when I needed cues.

Badly.

Not because she could not read.

Because she read every character as Lyssa.

The young wife sounded like Lyssa.

The brother sounded like Lyssa.

The servant sounded like Lyssa with less patience.

"You are ruining the company," I said.

"Line."

I gave her the line.

We reached scene two.

One of the missing three returned when she gave me the cue.

The next did not.

She read it.

I repeated it.

"Again," she said.

I repeated it again.

"From before."

"You have become Teren."

"No."

Correct.

We went from two lines earlier.

This time it stayed.

The last missing line was near the end.

I knew the joke before it.

I knew Hara's answer after it.

The middle remained blank.

Lyssa read it.

"That's stupid."

She looked at me.

"The line."

"Then remember it."

Cruel.

I said it twice.

Then once without looking.

Forty-three lines.

Probably.

Lyssa gave the pages back.

"Food."

I looked down.

I had eaten the bread.

"Done."

She checked the plate as though I might have hidden it.

"Good."

"I am developing a reaction to that word."

"Good."

She left for the north side.

I left for the theatre.

The walk gave me twenty minutes to discover that knowing forty-three lines at a table did not mean I knew forty-three lines while moving uphill on crutches.

I lost three.

Recovered two.

Lost another.

Recovered the first.

By the theatre door I had stopped counting because the number was becoming personal.

Nessa was inside.

Of course she was.

The stage was half lit. Davin was carrying a narrow bench. Jori had one knee on the floor beside the dinner table, tightening something beneath it.

Marek was not there yet.

This improved the morning briefly.

Nessa looked at me.

"Pell's still sick."

There it was.

"Fever?"

"Lower. His sister says he's eating."

"Good."

I heard myself.

Nessa did too.

Neither of us commented.

"Teren wants the whole piece after warm-up."

"Pages?"

"Available."

Not forbidden.

Available.

Different problem.

I put my coat away and went to the stage.

Jori stood.

"Mark's still yours."

I looked down.

The chalk mark from yesterday remained six inches wider than Pell's old one.

A little scuffed.

Still visible.

"For now," I said.

Jori had already gone back under the table.

That was apparently too much philosophy for furniture.

Marek arrived carrying nothing.

I distrusted this immediately.

"Where's the hat?" I asked.

"Nessa has it."

"Growth."

"I learned."

Nessa called from the wing, "You lost it after cleanup and I found it on the prop shelf."

Marek looked at me.

"Different kind of learning."

Teren arrived before I could answer.

He had coffee or something pretending to be coffee in a cup that did not belong onstage.

"Words?" he asked.

"Mostly."

"How mostly?"

"Forty-three in a room. Fewer while walking."

"Good."

I closed my eyes.

He said, "Start with scene two."

Of course.

Not scene one, where I was strongest.

Scene two.

We set.

Hara arrived while Nessa was checking the cups. She took one look at me in the Uncle's chair and said, "Still alive."

"Pell or me?"

"Both."

Useful.

The other actor joined us.

Marek took the Steward's tray.

Teren stood in the aisle.

"No pages unless you need them."

"That is a dangerous amount of freedom."

"Start."

We started.

Scene two began with Hara trying to leave.

Yesterday I had spent most of the scene trying not to forget Pell's words.

Today the first line arrived before I reached for it.

Then the second.

Then Hara answered and something changed.

Not much.

I heard her.

Actually heard her.

Yesterday her lines had been landmarks between mine.

Today they were accusations.

The Uncle had invited everyone to dinner and then spent the evening insisting that attendance meant agreement.

That was funny because he did not understand why anyone kept trying to leave.

I had known that yesterday.

Knowing and playing were apparently separate industries.

Hara said, "You cannot seat a person into consent."

I answered, "I can seat you into supper. The rest is your own bad judgment."

The line got no laugh because there was no audience.

But Hara's mouth changed.

She was no longer carrying me.

She answered harder.

I leaned back.

Not like Pell.

Pell leaned forward when the Uncle felt challenged. I had copied that yesterday because I had seen it a hundred times.

I leaned back because this Uncle did not think he was challenged yet.

He thought everyone else was being difficult in his house.

Hara stopped after the next exchange.

Teren did not.

We continued.

Marek entered.

Correct door.

Tray flat.

Red cup.

I took it without looking at him.

He waited.

Hara put hers back.

He left with everything.

Good Steward.

Still annoying.

The missing line came halfway through the scene.

I felt the blank open.

Yesterday I had looked empty and Hara had built me a bridge.

Today I knew where the pages were.

Side table.

Three steps.

I also knew the scene.

Hara wanted to leave.

The Uncle wanted her to stay because leaving would mean the dinner had failed and he had not yet admitted failure was possible.

The exact words remained gone.

I said, "Sit down. You can hate me after dessert."

Not the line.

Hara stared at me for half a beat.

Then answered with her actual next line.

"I have managed both at once so far."

The scene continued.

Teren let it.

That worried me more than stopping would have.

We finished scene two.

"Again," he said.

I looked at him.

"From where?"

"The missed line."

I went to the pages.

Found it.

Read it.

"Oh."

The actual line was better.

Annoying profession.

"Again," Teren said.

We took it from two lines earlier.

This time I had the words.

Hara answered.

The scene moved.

Teren said, "Keep the first one tonight if you lose it again."

I stared at him.

"My wrong line?"

"Your replacement line."

"It was worse."

"Yes."

"Then why keep it?"

"Because stopping is worse."

Specific.

Not permission to rewrite the play.

I nodded.

He took a drink.

"Again from the top."

We ran the whole piece.

I lost no lines in scene one.

In scene two I used the correct line.

In scene three I discovered a new problem.

I was early.

Not on an entrance.

On everything.

Yesterday I had waited for words because I needed them to arrive.

Today I knew them, so I started stepping on the ends of other people's lines.

Teren stopped us the third time.

"Greg."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"I'm early."

"Why?"

"Because I know what comes next."

"Then stop proving it."

Hara looked at the ceiling.

I pointed at her.

"You enjoyed that."

"Very much."

Teren said, "Again."

We went again.

I waited.

Not theatrically.

Just long enough for the other person to finish having their line.

Remarkable technology.

The scene improved.

Then I overcorrected and left a hole large enough for Marek to look toward the wing.

"Not that long," Teren said.

"Useful range."

"Find it."

We did.

By midday, I could get through the play without pages.

Not perfectly.

Without pages.

That distinction mattered.

Teren called break.

I sat on the edge of the stage with my crutches beside me and drank water.

Marek sat two feet away.

"You sound different."

I looked at him.

"From yesterday?"

"From Pell."

There it was.

I waited for the insult.

He ate something from a paper twist.

"Pell sounds angrier."

"The Uncle is angry."

"Later."

I thought about it.

Pell's Uncle entered irritated.

Mine entered certain.

Neither choice was necessarily better.

One belonged to Pell.

The other had happened because I had stopped copying him.

Marek held out the paper twist.

Nuts.

I took two.

"Thanks."

"Mine is better."

"Your Steward?"

"Yes."

"Than mine?"

"Yes."

I chewed.

"Explain."

"I don't talk as much."

I nearly choked.

Hara walked past us.

"He's right."

"This company has become unsafe."

Marek looked delighted.

Then Nessa called him because one of the trays had a loose binding.

He went.

I watched him go.

He knew the route now.

He knew the cups.

He knew to wait for Hara's return.

He had learned my role by watching me, then learned it again by doing it badly enough for Nessa to correct him.

That was how most things worked here.

I had simply been on the other side of it yesterday.

Rinna arrived during the afternoon run.

She listened from the back for half a scene, then left to speak with someone at the side door.

I recognized the lamp-glass seller when she came farther inside.

Not because she had become important.

Because I had bought lamp glass from her and Carrow was becoming full of people I could place.

She and Rinna spoke quietly near the door.

I heard none of it.

Good.

I was currently supposed to be ruining a dinner.

We finished the run.

Rinna was alone again by the time I came offstage.

She had a small wrapped parcel in one hand.

"Glass?" I asked.

"No."

That was the entire answer.

I did not ask again.

This required less effort than it once would have.

Maybe I was becoming old.

No.

Different problem.

Before doors opened, Teren gave me one note.

"Don't make him cleverer than he is."

I frowned.

"I'm not."

"You are starting to enjoy being right."

"The Uncle is right about some things."

"Yes."

"Then?"

"He thinks that means he's right about the room."

I considered that.

Hara was nearby adjusting a sleeve.

I looked at her.

"Are you going to enjoy this too?"

"Already am."

Fine.

Teren pointed toward the stage.

"He wants the dinner to work. Let him want that."

That I understood.

No life lesson.

Dinner.

I could do dinner.

The audience came in.

Not full.

Not thin.

Enough people to make the room become performance instead of rehearsal.

The Second Toast was second on the bill tonight.

I waited backstage with the Uncle's hat on my head.

Nessa had adjusted it again because yesterday's folded cloth had shifted.

"Better?" she asked.

I moved my head once.

"Yes."

"Don't give it to Marek."

"I have learned."

Marek said from behind me, "That's mine."

"No," Nessa and I said together.

He looked offended.

Then we were called.

I took the chair.

Crutches against the stool.

Right foot on Jori's mark.

Pages on the side table.

I had asked Nessa to leave them there.

Not because I expected to need them.

Because removing them to prove I did not need them would have been stupid.

Progress.

The lights shifted.

We began.

The opening line came.

Then the next.

I did not think about Pell.

That was new.

The first scene moved around the table.

The Uncle corrected the seating.

Hara ignored him.

He corrected it again.

Someone in the audience laughed before the chair gag arrived.

Small laugh.

Mine.

I felt it.

Dangerous.

I did not chase it.

The scene kept moving.

Marek entered through the correct door.

Tray flat.

Blue cup.

I took it.

He left with everything.

No one applauded his tray.

Good theatre.

Scene two.

Hara tried to leave.

I told her she could not seat a person into consent.

No.

She told me that.

For one horrifying instant the lines crossed in my head.

Then she said hers.

I answered mine.

Clean.

The audience laughed at the next exchange.

The missing line approached.

I knew it was coming.

That almost made it worse.

Hara gave me the cue.

The actual line arrived.

I said it.

No rescue.

No replacement.

We moved on.

That should not have felt as good as it did.

It did.

Scene three.

I waited for the other actor to finish.

Not too long.

Just enough.

Teren had somehow made pauses measurable without numbers.

The final toast approached.

I stood on the wider mark.

Hara's timing shifted around my cross.

Not to save me.

Because this was now the timing we had rehearsed.

The Uncle raised his cup.

For the first time since Pell had gotten sick, I was not trying to get through Pell's role.

I was playing the fucking scene.

The line landed.

Hara answered.

The other actor cut in.

The dinner collapsed exactly as written.

The audience laughed.

We finished.

Applause.

Ordinary again.

Maybe a little stronger.

I could not tell from inside it.

That was probably healthy.

Backstage, Nessa took the hat.

I gave it to her immediately.

"Growth," I said.

"Minimum standard."

Marek put down the tray.

"I was better."

"You were quieter."

"Exactly."

Hara came through.

I looked at her.

She said, "You didn't need me."

There were several answers available.

Most of them annoying.

"Not tonight."

She nodded once.

Then added, "You were early in three."

There it was.

"Once."

"Twice."

"One was enthusiasm."

"Two."

She left.

Teren found me after the next piece.

I was moving a chair with Jori.

He waited until we set it down.

"Better."

One word.

I wanted more.

This was embarrassing.

"How?"

He looked at me.

Apparently I had requested a note and would now suffer the consequences.

"Yesterday you knew where the play went. Today you were in it."

I waited.

"And?"

"And you were early twice."

Hara had infected him.

"Anything else?"

"Don't ask for praise until I invent some."

He walked away.

Jori picked up the chair again.

I helped him.

That should have annoyed me more.

It did not.

Rinna paid after cleanup.

Same arrangement as yesterday.

Marek received the Steward share.

I received the Uncle's share for the piece plus the rest of my work.

Another slightly better day of money.

Two days did not become a salary.

Pell's fever did not become my opportunity simply because I benefited from covering him.

Still.

The coins were real.

I put them away.

Rinna said, "Pell's sister thinks tomorrow or the day after."

"Good."

"You can stop saying it like you're surprised."

"Everyone has been using it against me."

"No one is using good against you."

"That's what makes it effective."

She had already moved on to Marek's pay.

Outside, the night was colder than yesterday.

I took the wider route home.

My head was tired in a way Hessa's experiments did not produce.

Not pain.

Crowded.

Forty-three lines.

Three scenes.

A wider chalk mark.

Hara changing timing around my cross.

Marek learning the Steward.

Two days of better pay.

Pell getting better somewhere else.

The needle case did not occur to me until I was almost home.

That seemed worth noticing.

Then I noticed that I had noticed it, which ruined the achievement.

At home, Lyssa was there.

The darker spool was not.

Neither was the reddish-brown sample.

The brown cloth remained folded near the wall with three pins.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads.

I took out the pages.

Lyssa looked at them.

"Need?"

"No."

"Then why have them?"

I considered this.

"Insurance."

She nodded.

I put them on the table.

Then I took out my pay and put it with the rest.

More than yesterday morning.

Still not enough to become careless.

Enough that the difference existed.

Lyssa was heating something in the pan.

"Pell?" she asked.

"Better. Probably back tomorrow or the day after."

"You?"

I sat.

"Better too."

She looked over.

I waited for it.

"Good," she said.

# CHAPTER 252

## THE WASHER

The sheets needed washing.

This was not a metaphor.

Nothing had happened to them except two people sleeping in them for several nights, which turned out to be enough.

Lyssa stripped the bed while I was still deciding whether being awake counted as participation.

One corner came free and hit me in the face.

I sat up.

"Violence."

"Move."

"I am moving."

"You are sitting."

"Movement begins internally."

She pulled the sheet from under me.

That settled the philosophy.

The room looked slightly wrong without the bed made. Not empty. Exposed.

The Uncle's pages were still on the table where I had put them last night.

I looked at them once.

No one had knocked.

No theatre runner waited outside.

Pell might be back today. He might not. Teren had not asked me to appear before the ordinary call, and ordinary call was later.

For the first time in two mornings, I did not have forty-three lines trying to climb into my head before breakfast.

This should have felt restful.

Instead Lyssa dropped the second sheet on my lap.

"Wash."

I looked down.

"All of it?"

"Sheets. Towels. Shirts."

"Today?"

She looked toward the window.

The sky was pale and dry.

"Yes."

Apparently weather had made a decision.

I stood.

My right shoulder still carried a small amount of yesterday. Not pain. Not enough to matter. Just the ordinary complaint of two days spent using crutches, rehearsing, standing, sitting badly, and sleeping with pages beside my hand like a man under siege by dialogue.

Hands fine.

Right leg fine.

Residual limb fine.

Both crutch grips normal.

The household had no emergency.

That was when households became most dangerous.

They found maintenance.

Lyssa had already separated the washing into two bundles.

One held the sheets and towels.

The other held clothes.

My damaged shirt was in the clothes pile.

Three loose threads still hung from the cuff.

I picked it up.

"Wash this?"

"Yes."

"The threads?"

"Still threads."

Useful.

The long-standing brown cloth remained folded near the wall with the same three pins.

Not washing.

Not my business.

The reddish-brown sample was still absent.

The darker spool was still absent too.

Also not my business.

I put the shirt back in the pile.

Lyssa tied the first bundle.

Then the second.

The sheet bundle was large enough to become architecture.

I looked at it.

Then at my crutches.

Then at Lyssa.

"No."

She tied the second knot.

"You haven't tried."

"I have eyes."

"You have a strap."

That was worse because she was right.

We owned a broad carrying strap that had previously been used for bundles, market loads, and one chair leg that had become briefly more important than dignity.

Lyssa threaded it around the larger bundle.

I tested the weight.

Dry cloth was not heavy.

Dry cloth was bulky.

Bulky was its own species of problem when both hands belonged to crutches.

I could sling the bundle high behind my shoulder.

That interfered with the left crutch.

Lower across my back.

That interfered with my hip.

In front.

Absolutely not.

Lyssa watched the experiment.

"Smaller."

"That was my next conclusion."

"Eventually."

She untied the bundle and divided the sheets from the towels.

Three bundles became manageable.

Annoying.

Manageable.

I could take one strapped behind me and one smaller bundle hanging from the right crutch below the grip, leaving the left hand free except for the left crutch, which was already a full-time occupation.

Lyssa took the third.

"You're coming?"

"Until the court."

"Then?"

"North side."

There it was.

Her day had not rearranged itself around laundry.

The laundry had been fitted into the route she already had.

Adult technology again.

We ate.

No Hessa note waited under the cup.

No Vale runner arrived.

No one asked me to investigate a mark on a needle case I had not bought.

I did not think about the needle case for almost the entire breakfast.

Then I did because I had just thought about not thinking about it.

Excellent.

The sheets won.

Outside, Carrow had that cold dry brightness that made every wet stone look innocent.

The wash court sat two streets below the west market, behind a row of buildings I had passed often enough that I knew the smell before I knew the entrance.

Soap.

Wet cloth.

Hot water.

A little ash.

I had known there was washing somewhere.

Of course there was washing somewhere.

Cities did not become cities by everyone individually discovering water.

I had simply never needed the place badly enough to care where the entrance was.

Lyssa turned through a wide arch.

I followed.

The court was larger than I expected.

Stone underfoot.

Open sky above most of it.

A roofed edge along one wall where people had set baskets, soap, wooden paddles, buckets, and folded dry things.

Three long basins ran through the middle, fed from a covered channel at one end.

The water in the nearest basin steamed slightly.

The second did not.

The third looked cold enough to hold a grudge.

Lines crossed the far half of the court between posts and wall hooks.

Most were already occupied.

Sheets moved above us like pale flags belonging to a nation founded on chores.

"Which one?" I asked.

Lyssa pointed.

"Hot first."

"Obviously."

She looked at me.

"That was confidence, not knowledge."

"Good."

I closed my eyes.

The word had followed me home from the theatre and now entered public infrastructure.

There were perhaps twenty people in the court.

Mostly women.

Two men.

One older boy carrying buckets.

A little girl sitting on a basket and kicking her heels against the side.

Nobody looked surprised to see me.

One woman looked at the bundle hanging from my crutch and said, "That'll drag."

I looked down.

It was not dragging.

Yet.

"Optimist."

She pointed at the next stretch of floor.

A shallow dip crossed the stones.

I took two steps.

The bundle touched.

Fine.

I lifted the loop higher on the crutch shaft.

"Thank you."

She had already turned back to a shirt in the basin.

Lyssa found an open place along the roofed wall.

We set the bundles down.

I expected instruction.

She took out the soap.

Handed it to me.

"Sheets first."

"That is instruction."

"Yes."

Then she opened her own smaller bundle and pulled out two pieces of cloth that were not ours.

I looked.

Not reddish-brown.

Not the pinned brown cloth from home.

Something pale and narrow.

I stopped looking.

Progress.

Lyssa wet one piece at the edge of the hot basin.

"You're washing work?"

"Rinsing."

Different thing.

I did not ask why.

She did not explain.

I put the first sheet into the water.

The sheet immediately became six times heavier and personally opposed to my existence.

"Ah."

The woman beside me glanced over.

"First sheet?"

"First hostile sheet."

She laughed.

Lyssa did not.

She had probably known.

Wet cloth changed the geometry.

That was obvious in the abstract.

In practice it meant I could not lean over the basin the way everyone else did without giving up one crutch, and I could not give up one crutch casually because the floor was wet stone and my right foot was currently my only foot.

I set both crutches against the basin.

Bad.

They slid.

I caught one before it fell.

The older boy carrying buckets said, "Hooks."

I looked behind me.

Iron hooks had been set into the posts under the roof.

Several already held baskets and handles.

One was empty.

I put the crutches there.

Both.

Then stood with my right hand on the basin edge.

Stable enough.

Not elegant.

Useful.

The sheet floated with one corner escaping toward another person's washing.

I grabbed it.

"Stay."

The sheet did not respect authority.

Lyssa rinsed her second piece.

Then came over and pushed the far corner back toward me.

"Fold it."

"In the water?"

"Yes."

I folded.

The entire sheet became smaller and worse.

She showed me once.

Not a lesson.

Just two hands doing the motion.

Fold into the water.

Press.

Soap the worst areas.

Work it against itself.

Open.

Shift.

Again.

I copied her.

My first attempt mostly moved water onto my shirt.

The second worked.

The woman beside me said, "Too much soap."

I looked at the soap.

Then at the sheet.

White suds had begun collecting along the fold.

"How much is too much?"

"That."

Precise local science.

I stopped adding soap.

Lyssa had already finished her rinse.

She squeezed the narrow cloth between both hands, wrapped it in another dry piece, and put it back into her bag.

"That's it?"

"That's it."

She checked the position of my crutches on the hook.

Then the sheet.

Then me.

"Cold after."

"Hot, then cold."

"Rinse."

"Yes."

She took her bag.

I stared.

"You are abandoning me."

"You're washing."

"This is how people die."

"In sheets?"

"History is broad."

She kissed my cheek.

The woman beside me pretended not to notice with the skill of someone who had noticed everything.

Lyssa said, "Don't leave them wet."

"I understood that independently."

"Good."

"Go."

She went.

I watched her cross the court, avoid a bucket without looking down, and disappear through the arch toward the north-side route.

Then I turned back to the sheet.

Still there.

No escalation.

Excellent.

The next hour taught me that washing sheets was not difficult enough to be interesting and not easy enough to disappear.

It occupied exactly the amount of attention required to make thinking about other things inconvenient.

Soap.

Fold.

Press.

Shift.

Rinse.

The first sheet went into the cold basin after I had squeezed enough water from it that moving it did not feel like transporting a drowned sail.

I used the basin edge for balance and kept the crutches on the hooks.

The older boy objected when I dripped across his bucket route.

Not verbally.

He stopped.

Looked at the trail.

Looked at me.

I moved the sheet closer to the stone.

"Sorry."

He continued.

The second sheet went faster.

Not because I had become a master washer.

Because I stopped inventing new ways to hold it.

That was competence often enough.

The towels were easier.

The clothes were easier still until I reached the damaged shirt.

Three loose cuff threads.

Still three.

I wet it.

The threads darkened with the cloth and stuck to my fingers.

For a moment I thought about cutting them.

I had no reason to.

I left them.

Soap did not require repair.

The blue paint streak on my better shirt had faded before today.

Washing made it paler.

Not gone.

I scrubbed once.

Twice.

The streak remained.

I considered the amount of effort required to make my shirt pretend theatre had never touched it.

Then stopped.

Pale blue was fine.

A woman farther down the basin was arguing with a teenage boy about a red stain on trousers.

"You put it there."

"I was wearing them."

"That is not a defense."

"It happened while I was wearing them."

"Exactly."

I minded my own business.

Mostly.

The little girl on the basket had acquired a wooden spoon.

Nobody seemed certain from where.

She hit the basket with it in a regular rhythm.

The older boy carrying buckets told her to stop.

She stopped until he turned away.

Then resumed more quietly.

Society.

By the time everything was washed, my shoulders had become aware of the day.

Not injured.

Worked.

Different from theatre.

Different from Hessa's chair.

Different from walking Carrow.

Wringing cloth wanted both hands, which meant I had to stand supported against the basin edge or sit.

I chose sitting for the sheets.

A low stone bench ran under the roof.

I sat with a sheet across my lap and twisted one section at a time.

An older woman at the other end watched me do this badly for perhaps thirty seconds.

Then said, "Other way."

I looked at my hands.

"Which other way?"

She stood.

Took the far end of the sheet.

"Hold."

I held.

She twisted her end clockwise.

I had been twisting mine clockwise too.

Which produced a thick rope of cloth that mostly moved the same water around.

"Opposite," she said.

I twisted counterclockwise.

Water ran onto the stones.

"Oh."

She let go.

"Better."

"Significantly."

She sat.

No name.

No biography.

No revelation.

A person in a wash court had known how to wring a sheet.

The world survived without becoming my network.

I finished the rest correctly.

Then came the lines.

Drying lines, not Uncle lines.

Important distinction.

Most of the lower ones were full.

Two higher lines had space.

I could reach them.

Technically.

Reaching while balancing on one right leg and trying to hold wet cloth above shoulder height was a bad definition of technically.

I looked around.

A short wooden pole leaned against one post with a forked end.

Ah.

I used the pole to lift the line down into reach.

That worked for the first sheet.

For the second, I lifted too quickly and knocked another person's cloth loose from its peg.

It fell.

Not into mud.

Onto stone.

Still wet.

Still my fault.

"Shit."

The owner turned.

I picked it up immediately.

"Sorry."

She looked at the cloth.

Then at the pole.

"Slow."

"Yes."

She rehung it.

No forgiveness ceremony.

No anger ceremony.

I went slower.

The sheets rose.

Towels followed.

Shirts.

Trousers.

The damaged shirt hung with its three threads visible at the cuff if anyone cared enough to inspect.

No one did.

I sat.

That was most of the job.

Which meant the job became waiting.

The court had a waiting population.

People mended things.

Talked.

Left and returned.

A woman peeled an apple with a small knife and shared pieces with two children.

Someone produced bread.

The bucket boy vanished and came back with another stack of buckets.

The little girl eventually abandoned the spoon and fell asleep against the basket.

I had brought no book.

No pages.

No food.

Poor planning.

I watched the sheets move.

My sheets.

Our sheets.

That distinction appeared without invitation.

Not mine because I had purchased them.

I had not.

Not ours because anyone had declared property law over the bed.

Ours because I knew which corner had the small worn patch and which towel had become too thin along one edge and which shirt would still have blue paint after it dried.

I knew where the wash court was now.

I knew the hot basin came first.

I knew the crutches went on the hooks instead of against wet stone.

I knew the forked pole existed.

I knew too much soap because too much soap looked exactly like my first sheet.

This was not impressive.

That was the point.

A man could spend an old life crossing bad country, surviving fights, remembering creatures that could kill him, learning roads that no longer existed, and then in a second life discover that wet sheets had logistics.

The sheets did not care.

Good for them.

I waited.

At some point the woman who had warned me about the dragging bundle left.

At some point the older woman left.

At some point two new people arrived and took their places without the court changing identity.

The sun crossed enough sky that the first sheet stopped looking wet.

I tested a corner.

Damp.

Not wet.

The second was worse.

I waited longer.

Theatre call would come eventually.

If someone wanted me.

No one had come looking.

I did not go looking either.

That felt strange for perhaps ten minutes.

Then less strange.

By the time I took the first shirts down, the blue streak had dried into a faint line.

Still there.

I smiled at it.

Not sentiment.

Just recognition.

The damaged shirt's threads had dried crooked.

Three.

Still three.

I folded it badly.

Refolded it less badly.

The towels came down.

Then the sheets.

Dry enough.

Not perfect.

Dry enough that carrying them home would not create a new problem.

I tied the bundles smaller this time.

Practice from the morning helped.

One on the strap behind me.

One on the right crutch.

Towels under the arm only until I realized that was stupid.

I retied them too.

The older boy was back.

He looked at the right-crutch bundle.

Then at the dip in the floor.

I lifted it before reaching the dip.

He nodded.

I felt absurdly rewarded.

Outside the arch, the city had continued without supervision.

Market traffic.

A dog sleeping beside a wall.

Two laborers moving boards.

Someone shouting about fish from far enough away that I refused responsibility.

I took the wider route home.

The clean sheet bundle shifted once.

I stopped.

Adjusted it.

Continued.

No one chased me.

No one offered work.

No strange object revealed itself.

No future memory opened.

No magical creature crossed the road.

No debt collector stepped from an alley.

The day remained washing.

At home, the room still looked wrong without the bed made.

I put the bundles down.

My shoulders thanked me by hurting slightly less.

I made the bed.

This was harder alone than washing the sheet had been.

One corner.

Across.

Back.

The far side required going around because I could not simply lean across a bed and trust two legs I did not have.

I went around.

Tucked.

Returned.

The sheet came loose from the first corner.

I stared at it.

"Enemy."

I fixed it.

The second sheet went on.

Blanket.

Done.

The room returned to itself.

Clean towels on the shelf.

Clothes folded.

Damaged shirt back on the shelf, three loose threads.

Better shirt folded with its paler blue paint streak.

The brown cloth remained where it had been all day.

Three pins.

I washed my hands.

The water in the basin clouded faintly with soap that had already been on me for hours.

Excellent.

Then I sat on the edge of the newly made bed.

That lasted perhaps thirty seconds.

The clean sheet felt too good.

I lay back.

Only for a moment.

I woke when Lyssa opened the door.

The light had changed.

She stood inside with her work bag.

I sat up.

"Maintenance injury."

"You slept."

"Severe."

She looked at the bed.

Then the folded clothes.

Then the towels.

"Dry?"

"Dry enough."

She touched the nearest towel.

Apparently evidence mattered in every profession.

"Good."

I pointed at her.

She smiled.

Then she took off her coat.

I asked, "North side?"

"Yes."

That was the whole report.

She did not explain the pale cloth she had rinsed.

I did not ask about the missing sample or spool.

She looked toward the table.

The Uncle's pages were still there.

"Called?"

"No."

"Pell?"

"Don't know."

She nodded.

No tragedy.

No opportunity.

Just don't know.

I stood and started supper because one of us had to.

Lyssa sat for a while before helping.

We ate on clean towels we did not need, beside clean shirts we were not wearing, in a room that smelled faintly of soap.

Nothing had advanced.

That was not true.

The wash court was two streets below the west market.

Hot first.

Cold rinse.

Crutches on the hooks.

Lift the line slowly.

Three loose threads remained three.

Blue paint remained blue, only paler.

The bed was clean.

That was enough for one day.
# CHAPTER 253

## THE STEWARD

Pell came back looking terrible.

This was reassuring.

Not because I wanted him terrible.

Because terrible and standing in the theatre doorway was considerably better than fever and absent.

He had lost enough color that his face looked borrowed. His hair had been tied back badly, his coat hung a little loose at the shoulders, and Nessa had one hand against his chest before he got three steps inside.

"No."

Pell stopped.

"I am here."

"Yes."

"I can work."

"No."

He looked past her toward the stage.

I was sitting on the edge with Jori, holding one end of a narrow rail while he checked a split near the foot.

Pell saw me.

Then saw Marek carrying a tray.

Then saw the tray.

His face changed.

"The Second Toast?"

Marek looked down at the tray as though surprised to discover evidence in his hands.

"No."

Nessa said, "Also no."

Pell frowned.

"What is no?"

"You performing."

"I came to perform."

"You came to stand in my doorway and look sick."

"I am not sick."

Nessa looked at him.

Pell corrected himself.

"Not fever sick."

"Excellent distinction. Go home."

He did not.

Of course he did not.

I had not been called to The Second Toast either.

That was the important part.

The tray in Marek's hands belonged to a different piece. The Uncle's hat was nowhere visible. Pell's pages were not on the side table. Teren was working with Hara and Venn near a painted doorway I did not recognize.

The two-day emergency had ended without waiting for Pell to return and announce it.

The bill had changed.

Good.

Probably.

I put my attention back on the rail.

Jori pressed his thumb against the split.

"Open."

I pulled lightly.

The split opened.

"Bad?"

"Wood."

"Strong diagnosis."

He took the rail from me and set it flat.

"Glue."

Davin, somewhere behind us, said, "Already."

Jori looked over.

Davin was holding the glue pot.

"Growth," I said.

Davin pointed at me with the brush.

"Was getting it before he asked."

"Dangerous independence."

Pell was still arguing with Nessa.

Quietly now.

That made it more serious.

"I walked here."

"Congratulations."

"I can sit."

"At home."

"I know the piece."

"Which piece?"

That stopped him.

Nessa pointed toward the stage.

"Not yours today."

Pell looked.

Teren had Hara cross through the painted doorway, stop, turn, and cross back.

Venn followed with a folded coat over one arm.

No Uncle.

No dinner table.

No Steward.

Pell exhaled.

Some part of him had apparently expected the theatre to preserve his absence as a hole.

I understood that more than I wanted to.

Two weeks ago, maybe even one week ago, I would have watched his face and tried to solve it.

Say something useful.

Tell him the show had gone well.

Tell him his role had survived.

Tell him I had not stolen anything.

All terrible options.

I held the rail while Jori worked glue into the split.

Pell said, "What am I doing?"

Nessa answered, "Going home."

"Tomorrow?"

"Ask tomorrow."

He looked toward Rinna.

Rinna was at the front table counting something that had nothing to do with his emotional needs.

He went to her anyway.

Healthy theatre.

Jori wrapped cord around the glued foot.

"Hold."

I held.

The morning had claimed me before I arrived.

Not dramatically.

I had gone to the theatre because I had spent yesterday washing our sheets and because the ordinary call existed whether anyone sent a boy to my door or not. The Uncle pages had stayed home on the table.

I had considered bringing them.

Then had not.

Insurance was useful until it became luggage.

At the theatre, Jori had pointed at the rail.

That had been enough.

My body was ordinary after the wash court. Shoulders fine after sleep. Right hand fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left tip normal. Both grips normal. The clean better shirt had a pale blue streak on one sleeve that had survived washing and apparently intended to outlive me.

I wore it.

Nobody cared.

Jori tied the cord.

"Done."

"Already?"

"Glue isn't."

"Then not done."

He looked at me.

"Rail work done."

Apparently completion had departments.

We set the rail under the rear overhang where nobody would kick it.

Davin put the glue away.

Then immediately took it back out because Jori pointed at a loose corner on a painted box.

Theatre maintenance reproduced when observed.

I stood.

Pell was at Rinna's table now.

She was not comforting him.

Good.

I could hear enough to know she was asking whether he had eaten.

He said yes.

She asked when the fever had broken.

He said yesterday morning.

She asked whether his sister knew he had walked here.

He said something quieter.

Rinna looked at him.

Pell looked at the floor.

Excellent.

Nessa called, "Greg."

I turned.

She held a narrow leather case.

Not mine.

Not magical.

Not a needle case.

Just a leather case long enough to hold stage knives.

"Rear shelf."

I took it.

That was the entire assignment.

I carried it to the rear shelf.

When I came back, Pell was sitting in the third row with a cup in both hands.

Still here.

Not working.

Compromise had entered the building.

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

"Alive," I said.

"Unfortunately."

"Good."

His eyes narrowed.

"I was gone three days."

"Two performances."

"Three days."

"Yes."

He looked toward the stage.

"How bad?"

There were several possible meanings.

I chose the one I could answer.

"First day I knew maybe a third of your exact words."

Pell closed his eyes.

"Rinna let you go on?"

"Teren did."

"Worse."

"Hara carried me."

"Of course."

"Second day was better."

He opened his eyes.

"How much better?"

"I knew the words."

"That is the minimum."

"Nessa said something similar."

He drank.

I waited.

He looked at Marek, who had now put down the tray and was helping Venn move a chair.

"Marek did Steward?"

"Yes."

"How bad?"

"First day?"

"Yes."

"Correct doors by the end."

Pell stared at me.

"That bad."

"He also learned the cups."

"Blue and red?"

"Yes."

"That is not difficult."

"You say that because you have never been Marek."

Pell considered this.

"Fair."

He looked at me again.

"Did you copy me?"

There it was.

Not accusation exactly.

Close.

"At first."

His mouth tightened.

"Teren stopped me."

"Good."

I pointed at him.

"Hostile recovery."

"What did he say?"

"That I knew what the man wanted. Play that. Don't imitate you."

Pell looked toward the empty stage chair that was not the Uncle's chair.

"And?"

"And apparently my Uncle thinks he owns the room longer than yours does."

Pell frowned.

"What does mine think?"

"That everyone has already disappointed him."

"Correct."

"Marek said you sound angrier."

"Marek is an idiot."

"Also correct."

Pell drank again.

That was enough discussion of the Uncle.

No pages.

No demonstration.

No request that I prove anything.

Pell sat sickly in the third row and I went back to work.

The new piece was called The Borrowed Coat.

I learned this because Nessa told me to stop putting the brown coat on the wrong hook.

Not the dangerous brown coat.

A stage coat.

Different brown.

This one had a patched elbow, a broad collar, and three brass-colored buttons, only two of which matched.

It belonged to Venn in the first piece and Hara in the second.

That was the problem.

Not for the audience.

For us.

The two pieces were paired close enough that Venn came offstage, took off the coat, and Hara needed it before the next piece began.

Nessa had arranged the change beside the left costume rack.

Venn off.

Coat off.

Hara in.

Simple.

Except the hook beside the rack already held a gray shawl, a belt, and one hat Marek had been told not to touch.

The brown coat kept disappearing into fabric.

Nessa moved the gray shawl.

Then the belt.

Then looked at the hat.

Marek appeared.

"No."

"I didn't do anything."

"Take your hat."

His face brightened.

"My hat."

"Take it to the other rack."

Less bright.

He took it.

The hook became visible.

Nessa put the coat there.

"Brown coat lives here between pieces."

I looked at it.

"Temporary residence."

"Greg."

"Here."

"You're on this side for the first piece."

"Property?"

"Coat."

I waited.

"Only coat?"

"And Venn's letter."

There it was.

Employment.

The Borrowed Coat was not complicated enough to deserve its title.

Venn played a man who had borrowed a coat to impress a woman and then discovered the coat belonged to her brother.

Hara played the woman.

Marek played the brother.

Of course.

My role was not in the play.

My job was to make sure Venn entered with the letter in the coat pocket and came off with both coat and letter accounted for.

Then the coat had to reach Hara for the next short piece, where it represented an entirely different coat belonging to an entirely different man.

Theatre did not respect property law.

Teren ran the first piece.

I stood by the left rack.

Venn came to me before his entrance.

"Letter."

I gave it to him.

He put it into the inside pocket.

I said, "Other pocket."

He stopped.

"Why?"

I knew why.

Because in rehearsal he had reached across his body for the letter and caught the broad collar under his chin.

Nessa had moved the letter to the outside pocket after that.

I had seen it.

Venn had apparently not.

"Outside."

He looked toward Nessa.

She was helping Hara with a cuff.

"Outside," she said without turning.

Venn moved the letter.

"Everyone knows my coat."

"Not your coat."

He looked at me.

"That is the play."

Right.

He went on.

I watched from the wing.

Not because I needed to admire him.

Because the coat had to come back.

Venn was good.

Not Hara good.

Different.

Quiet.

His character was trying very hard to appear wealthier than he was and kept making the mistake of protecting the borrowed coat from ordinary contact.

When Hara offered him a chair, he checked the back before sitting.

Small laugh.

When Marek entered and brushed past him, Venn turned sideways to protect the sleeve.

Bigger laugh.

Nobody explained the coat mattered.

His body did.

Teren had probably made him do that.

Or Venn had found it.

I did not know.

Healthy.

Halfway through the scene, Venn reached into the outside pocket and found the letter.

Correct.

Then Marek recognized one of the brass-colored buttons.

"You."

Venn froze.

Hara looked between them.

"What?"

Marek pointed at the coat.

"That button."

Venn looked down.

The audience laughed because looking down was guilt.

He tried to cover it by fastening the coat.

Wrong button.

The mismatched one would not pass through the tighter hole.

The audience laughed harder.

I had seen the button problem backstage.

I had not known it was the joke.

That felt useful.

The scene ended with Hara learning the truth, Marek demanding his coat back, and Venn refusing to remove it until he could leave the room without standing in shirtsleeves.

Reasonable.

Curtain.

Venn came off fast.

"Coat."

I held out both hands.

He shrugged out of it.

The letter remained in the pocket.

I checked.

Not because I distrusted him.

Because Nessa had told me to.

"Letter."

"Still there."

"I found it."

"Excellent."

I pulled it out and put it on the property table.

Then I put the coat on the hook.

Hara was already coming.

She had changed one outer layer and was fastening her hair differently.

"Coat."

I handed it to her.

She put it on.

The sleeves were too long for her by perhaps an inch.

Nessa folded each cuff once.

"Keep."

Hara flexed her hands.

"Fine."

Then she went.

Twenty seconds.

Maybe less.

The coat had been Venn's problem, then my object, then Hara's costume.

No speech.

Good.

Pell watched from the third row.

I noticed only because he laughed when Marek tried to retrieve the hat from the wrong rack and found a bonnet instead.

Marek came around the flat holding it.

"This is not mine."

Nessa said, "Evidence supports you."

Pell laughed hard enough to cough.

The room changed.

Nessa turned immediately.

So did Rinna.

Pell raised one hand.

"Fine."

Nobody believed him.

The cough stopped.

Rinna pointed at the door.

Pell stared.

"Seriously?"

"Yes."

"I walked here."

"You keep saying that like it improves the decision."

"It proves capacity."

"It proves poor judgment."

I looked at Hara's coat disappearing into the second piece.

Not my problem.

Pell's argument was also not my problem.

This was becoming a productive day.

He left five minutes later.

Not happily.

Nessa made Venn walk him partway.

Venn objected that he was in the next piece.

Nessa said he was not.

Venn checked.

He was not.

Apparently theatre could weaponize schedules for health.

Pell looked at me on the way out.

"Tomorrow."

"Maybe."

He pointed at me.

I smiled.

Rinna heard.

"Ask tomorrow."

Pell left.

The second piece continued.

Hara wore the brown coat as a widow's brother's coat or husband's coat or possibly a debtor's coat. I never learned because I was busy resetting the first piece's letter and helping Davin find a wooden stool that had migrated behind the curtain.

This did not bother me.

Not knowing every play had stopped feeling like a deficiency.

Mostly.

At midday, Rinna gave me bread and a piece of hard cheese because I had been there since morning.

I paid for neither.

I also received no philosophical explanation of company food.

Marek sat beside me on the stage edge.

"Steward."

I looked at him.

"What?"

"Mine was better."

"We settled this."

"Pell is back."

"Briefly."

"So Steward is yours again."

I ate cheese.

"Was it ever mine?"

Marek frowned.

"You did it first."

"That is not ownership."

"Then mine."

"Also not ownership."

He considered.

"Shared."

"Temporary employment."

"Too many words."

Hara passed us carrying the brown coat.

Not wearing it now.

She dropped it into my lap.

"Hook."

I looked at Marek.

"Authority."

He looked impressed.

I put the coat on the hook.

The afternoon was not a performance for me.

It was work.

I helped Jori test the repaired rail after the glue had set enough to handle.

Not enough to abuse.

He put it upright.

I held one side.

Davin pressed the foot.

No opening.

"Good."

I looked at Jori.

"Can we use it?"

"Tomorrow."

"Then why test it now?"

"So tomorrow isn't when we learn it failed."

Reasonable.

Annoying.

We set it aside.

Nessa had me carry three costume pieces from one rack to another because the first rack needed space for evening.

I could carry one at a time while using both crutches.

So I did.

Three trips.

Nobody combined them into a challenge.

On the second trip I passed the Uncle's hat.

It was on a high shelf.

Not hidden.

Not waiting for me.

A hat.

I kept walking.

That felt like the correct amount of meaning.

By late afternoon, Teren had me read four lines for a porter in a piece I had seen once.

Not because Pell was sick.

Not because I had covered Uncle.

Because the actor who usually did Porter was helping Jori move a painted stair unit and Teren wanted to hear the scene while the stage was clear.

I read from the page.

Standing at the wing.

No costume.

No audience.

Four lines.

The first was fine.

The second I put too much suspicion into.

Teren stopped me.

"Why do you think he knows?"

"Because the letter is false."

"Greg knows that."

Right.

I tried again.

The Porter took the letter because someone handed him a letter.

That was all.

Teren nodded.

Then the regular actor came back.

He took the page from me.

We continued with him.

No promotion.

No demotion.

No emotional ceremony.

I liked it.

Possibly because I had become less stupid.

Possibly because I had already had enough ceremony from sheets.

Rinna paid me the normal copper at the end of the day.

Normal.

Not Uncle share.

Not emergency share.

Marek got normal money for his actual work.

Hara got hers.

Venn had returned after delivering Pell and got paid for what he had done.

The company had no interest in preserving my two better-pay days as a new economic category.

Correct.

Still mildly disappointing.

I put the copper away.

Rinna said, "Pell's sister sent a boy."

I looked at her.

"He home?"

"Yes."

"Angry?"

"Apparently."

"Good."

Rinna looked at me.

I smiled.

She almost did.

"Tomorrow?"

I asked it because everyone did eventually.

Rinna looked at the evening board.

"Come ordinary."

That was new enough that I checked the words.

"Ordinary call?"

"Yes."

"Role?"

"Ask Teren."

"Work?"

She looked around the theatre.

There were chairs.

Coats.

Props.

A repaired rail.

Two flats waiting for evening.

Marek holding something he had almost certainly been told not to hold.

"Probably."

Fair.

I left.

Outside, Carrow had reached the hour where every cookshop smelled better than my purse wanted it to.

I bought a small hot cake anyway.

Money had come in.

Money went out.

The arithmetic existed without becoming a moral event.

I ate walking slowly.

The better shirt's pale blue streak caught the last light when I moved my arm.

Still there.

At home, Lyssa was already back.

The brown cloth remained folded near the wall.

Three pins.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

No Uncle pages on the table.

I stopped.

They were gone.

That got my attention.

Lyssa looked up from where she was sitting.

"Where are the pages?"

She pointed at the shelf.

I looked.

Folded there.

Beside my damaged shirt.

Not thrown away.

Not returned.

Moved.

"Why?"

"Food."

I looked at the table.

There was food.

Reasonable.

"The pages were in the way."

"Yes."

I took off my coat.

"Pell came back."

Lyssa looked at me.

"Good?"

"Terrible."

She waited.

"Looks terrible. Fever broke yesterday. Walked to theatre. Nessa and Rinna sent him home."

"Good."

"Correct."

I sat.

Lyssa pushed a bowl toward me.

I ate.

After several bites she asked, "Uncle?"

"No."

That was all.

She nodded.

I almost told her the bill had changed.

That Marek had not been Steward.

That I had spent most of the day managing one brown stage coat between Venn and Hara.

That Pell had asked whether I copied him.

That Teren had given me four Porter lines and then taken them away when the Porter returned.

None of it required a report.

I ate.

Lyssa had something pale folded near her work bag.

Not the pale rinse cloth from yesterday, maybe.

I could not tell.

I did not ask.

She did not ask whether I had checked the needle case.

Good household.

After supper, I took the Uncle pages from the shelf.

Not to study.

I folded them once more and put them inside my coat.

Lyssa watched.

"Need?"

"No."

"Then why?"

I considered saying insurance again.

It was no longer true.

"Return."

"Tomorrow?"

"Ordinary call."

She nodded.

I put the coat by the door.

The pages had been Pell's before they had been mine for two days.

Tomorrow they could become theatre paper again.

I knew forty-three lines I had not known three days ago.

Marek knew eleven Steward lines he had not known either.

Pell was home being angry under supervision.

The bill had changed.

The rail glue was drying.

The brown stage coat was on its hook.

Our sheets were clean.

Nothing had reset.

Nothing had become permanent just because it had happened twice.

That seemed like a useful kind of ordinary.
# CHAPTER 254

## THE USHER

The Uncle pages were in my coat.

That was the first thing I checked before leaving.

Not because I needed them.

Because I had decided to return them and had enough experience with theatre to know that deciding to return an object did not guarantee the object would participate.

Lyssa was already gone.

The long brown cloth remained folded near the wall.

Three pins.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

The pale thing from beside Lyssa's work bag was gone.

This told me exactly nothing except that objects continued having lives when I was not supervising them.

Healthy.

I ate bread.

Not the last bread.

Growth had occurred somewhere.

The better shirt still carried the pale blue streak on one sleeve. In morning light it looked less like paint and more like the memory of paint.

I wore it anyway.

My body had nothing new to report. Shoulders normal. Right hand normal. Right leg normal. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip ordinary. Both grips stayed where grips were supposed to stay.

No Hessa note.

No Vale runner.

No theatre emergency.

Only ordinary call.

That was enough.

Outside, Carrow was cold and bright enough to punish anyone who had believed yesterday's afternoon meant spring. The haircut remained excellent indoors and treacherous in wind.

I turned my collar higher around my neck and went west.

The theatre side door was open.

Nobody was waiting for me.

Good.

I went inside and nearly walked into a stack of benches.

Not because they were moving.

Because I was.

Jori had three of them turned sideways across the aisle while Davin checked the feet.

I stopped.

Davin looked up.

"Road."

"I am in a building."

"Still road."

I went around.

One bench had a chalk mark on the end.

Two short lines.

The other two did not.

I noticed.

I did not ask.

This felt unnatural.

Nessa came through the rear passage carrying two folded coats and a basket of cloth belts.

She saw me.

Then my coat.

Then my face.

"Pages?"

I took the Uncle pages out.

She shifted both coats to one arm and held out her hand.

I gave them to her.

That was it.

No ceremony.

No question about whether I had learned them.

No warning to forget them.

No statement that Pell owned them again.

Nessa folded the pages once along the existing crease and put them on the rear paper shelf beneath a stack of other scripts.

The Uncle disappeared into paper.

I still knew forty-three lines.

Both facts survived.

"Anything else?" I asked.

"Yes."

Of course.

She handed me the basket of belts.

"Costume rack."

I carried it to the costume rack.

Ordinary call remained honest.

When I came back, Rinna was at the front table with tickets arranged in four small stacks and one longer strip of paper beside them.

She looked up.

"Greg."

"Rinna."

"House."

I waited.

"Is that a role?"

"No."

"Good."

She pointed toward the front doors.

"First bill is selling heavier than yesterday. Kesh is late."

I had never met Kesh closely enough to know whether Kesh being late was a personality or an event.

"Who is Kesh?"

"The man who usually does what you're about to do."

Useful.

"What am I about to do?"

"Seat people."

I looked toward the house.

Benches.

Aisles.

Stage.

People not yet inside.

"That sounds easy."

Rinna looked at me.

I corrected myself.

"That sounds like something I have not done."

"Better."

She slid the long strip of paper toward me.

It was not a list of names.

Numbers.

Rows.

Small chalk marks beside some.

"Front two rows sold marked seats. Everything behind is open unless I tell you otherwise."

I looked at the benches.

"There are no numbers."

"Ends."

I went to the nearest bench.

A small chalk 3 sat low on the aisle end where I had never needed to look before.

"Ah."

"Tickets have row and place for the first two. After that, keep the center aisle clear and do not let six people turn one bench into eight."

"Strong civic standard."

"Also no standing in the side lane during performance."

"Why?"

"Actors use it."

I knew that side lane.

I had used it.

From backstage.

From the house it looked like empty wall.

Interesting.

Rinna continued.

"If someone asks for the end because they need the end, give them the end if you can."

I looked at her.

"Need how?"

"They'll tell you."

That was a better answer than the one I had been preparing.

"Tickets?"

"Bring them to me. You do not take money."

"Excellent."

"You also do not explain prices."

"Still excellent."

"You do not promise another show."

"Less excellent."

Rinna handed me three small chalk pieces.

"One for row marks if they rub. Two spare."

I stared at them.

"Authority."

"Chalk."

"Limited authority."

"Go check the house."

I went.

The first two rows had tiny place marks along the bench backs.

Not numbers exactly.

Short chalk divisions with small digits below them.

I had sat in this house dozens of times and never noticed because they had never mattered to me.

The third row had only the row number.

The fourth too.

The center aisle was wider than the side lanes.

I knew why from stage routes.

Now I knew why from audience movement.

Same floor.

Different job.

At the end of the second row, one chalk digit had blurred into something that might have been four or an accusation.

I rubbed it with my thumb.

Worse.

I looked at the chalk in my hand.

Then at Rinna.

She was already selling a ticket to a woman outside.

I considered improving the mark.

Dangerous word.

I waited until she finished.

"Second row, right side. Is that four?"

Rinna looked from the table.

"Five."

I looked again.

"That was not one of my options."

"Then your options were bad."

"Do I rewrite it?"

"Yes."

I wrote 5.

The number looked too large compared with the others.

I erased part with my thumb.

Now it looked wounded.

Davin passed behind me carrying a bench foot.

He looked.

"Art."

"Leave."

He did.

The doors opened before I felt ready.

This had also happened with acting.

Apparently buildings disliked confidence.

The first people came in slowly.

A couple with two tickets.

Row one.

Places two and three.

I checked the ticket.

Checked the bench.

Pointed.

"First row. Two and three."

The man looked at the stage.

"That close?"

I looked at the ticket.

"Yes."

"Can we sit back?"

I looked toward Rinna.

She was dealing with three people at the table.

The first two rows were marked because the seats had been sold specifically.

Everything behind was open.

Could they move back?

Probably.

Probably had become expensive in offices.

"Ask Rinna before I rearrange what you bought."

The woman laughed.

The man did not.

They went back to Rinna.

Excellent beginning.

The next group had no marked places.

Four people.

I sent them to the fourth row.

They chose the middle.

No problem.

Then a woman came in alone with a cane.

Not one of mine.

A real cane.

Dark wood, brass-colored cap, rubberless end.

Her ticket was open seating.

She stopped at the third row.

"End."

I looked at the empty bench.

Both ends open.

"Either."

"Right."

She took the right end.

That was easy enough.

Then she said, "Not that right."

I looked.

She pointed to the other side.

"Door side."

"Ah."

She crossed in front of me and sat on the left end, closer to the exit.

I had assumed right meant my right.

She had meant useful right.

Or maybe changed her mind.

The system survived.

A man behind her said, "Can I get past?"

She moved both knees aside.

He went.

I kept the center aisle clear.

For almost three minutes.

Then Marek entered carrying a wooden crate and stopped directly in it.

I stared at him.

He stared at me.

"What?"

"Center aisle."

"Backstage is blocked."

"House is opening."

"I am crossing."

"You are standing."

He looked down at the crate.

As though the crate might defend him.

Nessa shouted from the wing, "Marek."

He moved.

I had authority again.

Very specific authority.

Dangerous.

The first real seating mistake came from a family of five.

Mother.

Father.

Three children.

Open seating.

There was a bench in row five with enough visible room.

I pointed them there.

They went.

The youngest child climbed over the bench instead of around it.

The father caught him.

The mother sat.

Then an older man already at the far end said, "Those are taken."

I looked at the bench.

Nothing marked.

The mother looked at me.

I looked at the older man.

"Open seating."

He pointed at two folded scarves lying on the bench.

"Taken."

Scarves.

I had seen them.

I had interpreted them as cloth.

Technically correct.

Functionally wrong.

The mother looked at the remaining space.

Five people could fit if everyone became narrow and stopped owning elbows.

Not comfortably.

I said, "One row back."

She gathered the children.

No argument.

The father picked up one child.

They moved.

The older man said, "Sorry."

The mother said, "It's fine."

Nobody asked me to decide whether scarves could hold seats under theatre law.

Good.

I walked back to the door.

Rinna looked over.

"Problem?"

"Scarves have acquired property rights."

She glanced at row five.

"Ah. Those two are with the woman buying now."

"Open seating."

"Open when not held."

"That is a rule you omitted."

"I thought you knew cloth."

Hostile workplace.

The woman buying tickets came in.

She thanked the older man.

The scarves became people.

Evidence resolved.

The house filled unevenly.

Front rows first because people with marked tickets had already chosen certainty.

Then back rows because people without marked tickets often wanted distance.

Middle rows became complicated last.

I learned that couples preferred pretending one empty place beside them did not exist.

I learned that three children occupied either two seats or seven depending on emotional state.

I learned that people asking "Is this good?" did not want the same answer.

One man meant good view.

One woman meant good for leaving early.

A boy meant close enough to see Marek fall over if Marek fell over.

I could answer only the first by looking.

The second I moved toward an aisle.

The third I told the boy, "Statistically promising."

His father laughed.

Rinna heard.

"Do not promise falls."

"I promised probability."

"Greg."

"Fine."

Kesh arrived after the house was more than half full.

I knew him once I saw him.

I had seen him dozens of times.

That was embarrassing.

He was the broad man who sometimes stood near the front doors before performances and disappeared when the curtain opened.

Apparently I had categorized him as architecture.

He wore a dark vest and had a narrow strip of red cloth tied around one wrist.

He looked at the house.

Then at me.

"You're in my place."

"Late."

"Yes."

No defense.

He took the chalk from my hand.

Checked row two.

Stopped at my large wounded 5.

Looked at me.

"Five?"

"Eventually."

He rubbed it out and wrote a smaller 5 in one motion.

I disliked professionals.

Rinna called from the table, "Keep Greg through start."

Kesh nodded.

I had not been released.

He walked the front aisle once.

Moved one folded scarf.

Not the claimed scarves.

A different one that had fallen partly into the lane.

He checked the side lane.

Then opened the second front door wider.

I followed because apparently this was training now.

Not formal training.

Walking behind a man who knew where people were supposed to go.

"Center stays clear," he said.

"I know."

"Side stays clear after bell."

"I know."

He looked at my crutches.

Then at the side lane.

"You're fine there now. Not after."

"I know why."

"Good."

Everyone had that word.

A woman approached holding two tickets.

"Together?"

Kesh looked.

Different row marks.

"No."

She frowned.

"We bought together."

He looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked at the ticket backs.

Then at her stack.

"One copied wrong."

She crossed out the second row mark and rewrote it.

Kesh handed the tickets back.

"Now together."

No crisis.

Paper wrong.

Paper corrected by the person allowed to correct it.

I knew this religion.

The bell rang.

Not curtain.

First warning.

People in the doorway became urgent.

Kesh stopped letting them choose slowly.

"Open seats from row six back."

A group of three asked where.

He pointed once.

They went.

A man tried to stand at the rear wall.

Kesh said, "Bench."

"I prefer standing."

"Not there."

"Why?"

"Door."

The man sat.

No explanation of fire, flow, stage access, emergency, dignity, or civilization.

Door.

Useful language.

The second bell rang.

Rinna closed the ticket stack.

I thought I was done.

Kesh pointed to the left wall.

"Stay until opening."

"Why?"

"Late entry."

Of course.

The theatre had people who arrived after the theatre began.

I had known this from backstage only as door noise.

Now I became the door noise.

The lights lowered.

Not truly dark.

Dim enough.

The audience changed.

That was the strange part.

Five minutes earlier they had been coats, complaints, children, scarves, choices, knees, ticket marks, and people asking whether row four was good.

Then the stage lit.

They became a single quiet thing facing forward.

Not actually single.

Someone still coughed.

A child whispered.

A man in row seven adjusted his coat three times.

But the room had direction now.

I stood against the left wall with both crutches planted close and watched the stage from an angle I almost never used.

The first piece was The Doctor's Supper.

I knew it.

Hara as the physician.

Marek as the brother.

Pell was not in it today.

Another actor had the patient.

No announcement.

No emotional event.

The piece existed with the cast on the board.

Hara entered.

The audience settled another degree.

From backstage, laughter had always sounded like weather arriving through wood.

From here I could see where it started.

Not intellectually.

Physically.

Two people in the front row first.

Then three behind them.

Then the rest.

Marek said something stupid about medicine.

A woman near the center laughed before her husband did.

The laugh spread.

I caught myself watching the audience instead of the stage.

Kesh, beside the door, whispered, "Door."

I looked.

Two late people stood outside.

Right.

Employment.

I opened enough to let them in without throwing full street light into the house.

The man entered first.

The woman behind him stopped.

"Where?"

I looked at the dark benches.

This was harder now.

Empty places had become gaps between silhouettes.

Kesh pointed toward row eight.

Two seats at the end.

I led them only far enough to see.

The woman whispered, "Closer?"

I looked at Kesh.

He shook his head.

I whispered, "Not without crossing the front."

She accepted row eight.

The man did too.

They sat.

The door closed.

Onstage, Hara had reached the hunger line.

I knew because the audience broke.

I had missed the setup.

The laugh still worked without me.

Good.

For the rest of the first piece, late arrivals came in three small groups.

One wanted the front.

No.

One had a child already asleep against a shoulder.

Kesh found them an end.

One man insisted his brother was saving a place in row four.

He was.

A raised hand appeared from darkness.

We let him cross between scenes, not during.

That was apparently the rule.

I learned it by being stopped once when I started to wave him through.

Kesh touched my arm.

"Wait."

I waited.

Curtain.

Applause.

Then movement.

The brother crossed.

No speech.

The second piece required a fast reset.

This meant the audience became a problem again.

People stood.

Stretching.

Whispering.

One tried to leave by the side lane.

I caught him.

"Front."

He looked at the nearer side opening.

"That door."

"Stage route."

He looked through it.

Venn was already behind the flat holding a chair.

The man understood without needing philosophy.

"Front."

He went.

The little boy who had asked about Marek falling found me near the door.

"He didn't fall."

"First piece."

His father said, "Do not encourage him."

"I have been instructed similarly."

The boy looked hopeful about the second piece.

I refused to promise.

The reset finished.

Second bell.

People sat.

I stayed at the door.

The second piece was one I had never seen.

Good.

I watched more of it.

Not all.

Door.

Late people.

One woman leaving because she felt ill.

Not dramatic ill.

She said the room was too warm.

Kesh opened the outer door and let her stand in the entry until she felt better.

Her friend stayed with her.

I stood farther aside.

No medicine.

No Hessa.

No crisis.

Warm room.

When she returned, Kesh put her on the rear end instead of making her go back to the middle of row six.

No one objected.

I understood the rule after it happened.

Need the end if you need the end.

Rinna had said that.

The second piece was funnier than I expected.

Not because I understood the plot.

Because Hara entered late as somebody's aunt and changed the entire audience before she spoke.

I could see it now.

People recognized her.

Not celebrity.

Not fame.

Familiarity inside this room.

Bodies shifted.

Faces lifted.

A few people smiled before the line.

Then she gave them nothing for three beats.

The laughter came from anticipation collapsing under itself.

I had watched Hara do silence from backstage.

From the door, I watched the audience do the other half.

That was not my lesson.

It was simply visible from here.

I liked the door.

This concerned me.

After the second piece, Kesh said, "Done."

I looked at him.

"Already?"

"House work."

"You stay?"

"Evening."

"Now?"

"Reset later."

He handed me the chalk.

I looked at it.

"Why?"

"Rinna's."

Of course.

I returned the chalk to Rinna.

She was counting the unsold tickets.

"How bad?" she asked.

"Scarves can reserve seats."

"Yes."

"Kesh has handwriting that humiliates me."

"Yes."

"The left side door is not an audience door."

"Correct."

"Late people become invisible in the dark."

"Generally."

"People ask if seats are good without defining good."

Rinna looked up.

"Did the house fit?"

"Yes."

"Anyone left standing?"

"No."

"Anyone block the side?"

"Not after bell."

"Then fine."

That was the review.

No certificate.

No title.

No declaration that I had become front-of-house staff.

She handed me a folded stack of handbills.

"Rear table."

I carried them to the rear table.

Theatre preserved itself through insult.

The afternoon returned me to ordinary backstage work.

I moved two light props.

Held a flat while Jori changed a tie.

Took a costume bag upstairs one item at a time because the bag itself was too awkward with crutches.

Davin asked whether I had enjoyed being important.

"I controlled scarves."

"Power corrupts."

"You painted both sides of a sign the same."

"History."

Marek appeared wearing a hat.

Nessa called his name.

He took it off.

The world continued.

Pell did not appear.

Nobody discussed him.

That was probably the best available recovery.

Near late afternoon, Teren ran a short scene and asked me to stand in for one missing reader for six lines.

I read.

Not memorized.

No costume.

No role claim.

One line had a joke I could feel coming.

I almost leaned into it.

Then did not.

Teren stopped after the scene.

"Again tomorrow if I need it."

"Which part?"

"Reading."

"Strong career."

He was already walking away.

I smiled.

At the front, Kesh had gone.

The house was empty again.

I stood in the center aisle.

The benches looked ordinary.

Row five still held one forgotten scarf.

Not one of the reserved ones from morning.

Different scarf.

I picked it up.

Rinna had a small basket near the front table labeled FOUND.

Not with words.

With objects.

One glove.

A child's wooden ring.

A comb.

Two folded handkerchiefs.

I put the scarf in.

Then stopped.

"Does this reserve the basket?"

Rinna looked at me.

"No."

"Good."

She went back to writing.

I left before the scarf acquired a claimant.

Rinna paid me normal theatre money.

One ordinary day.

No emergency share.

No role share beyond the work she counted.

I did not ask whether house work paid differently because apparently it had not.

Money entered my purse.

The purse remained a purse.

Outside, Carrow was already cooling.

I bought bread.

Not because Lyssa had written a list.

Because we needed bread and I had eaten enough of the existing loaf to understand the future.

I bought onions too.

Two.

Then, thinking better of it, three.

The woman at the stall looked at me.

"Three."

"Yes."

"No paper today?"

"No."

"Growth."

Everyone in the city had learned the word.

I paid.

At home, Lyssa was not there yet.

The room looked ordinary.

Brown cloth.

Three pins.

Damaged shirt.

Three threads.

No Uncle pages in my coat.

That absence felt correct.

I put the bread on the table.

Onions beside it.

Then moved one onion because three in a row looked like I was conducting an experiment.

Lyssa came home after dark carrying a narrow wrapped bundle and a small paper twist.

She looked at the table.

"Three."

"Apparently tradition."

She put her things down.

"Work?"

"Theatre."

"Role?"

"No."

I considered the six read lines.

"Not really."

She waited.

I said, "I seated people."

That got more attention than I expected.

"You?"

"Hostile phrasing."

"Did they sit?"

"Mostly after instruction."

She smiled.

I told her about the scarves.

Only the scarves.

Not the entire architecture of late entry, side lanes, marked rows, open benches, audience movement, Hara's silence, or Kesh's superior 5.

Lyssa unwrapped the paper twist.

Dried herbs.

No connection to anything I understood.

"Reserved seats?" she asked.

"Apparently cloth can become law if everybody agrees."

She looked at the long brown cloth near the wall.

I followed her eyes.

Three pins.

Same fold.

I pointed.

"No."

She laughed.

Good.

We ate bread and onions with something she had brought in the wrapped bundle that turned out to be food.

This was an excellent development.

After supper, I hung my coat by the door.

Lighter without the Uncle pages.

Not physically enough to matter.

Still.

Tomorrow had no ordinary call written anywhere I owned.

Rinna had not told me to come.

Teren had said maybe reading if he needed it, which was not a call.

Kesh had not hired me into a new profession.

The house would open again whether I stood at the door or not.

I knew where row five was now.

I knew why the side lane stayed empty.

I knew a scarf could mean taken.

I knew late people entered through less light.

I knew none of this yesterday.

That was enough.

Theatre had not given me a role.

It had given me a door and then taken it back.

For one day, that was work.
# CHAPTER 255

## THE NEIGHBOR

Nobody came for me in the morning.

This was not an emergency.

It took me perhaps three minutes to believe that.

I ate bread with one of yesterday's onions and considered the shape of a day that had not already been assigned by Rinna, Teren, Hessa, Antonius Vale, a fever, a broken rail, or a household list.

The answer was apparently bread and onion.

Lyssa had left before I woke properly. Not secretly. Her work bag was gone, the cup she used in the morning was upside down beside the basin, and a short note sat under the edge of the bread board.

Back late.

Two words.

No destination.

No assignment for me.

The long brown cloth remained folded near the wall with the same three pins. My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with the same three loose threads. The pale work material from two mornings ago remained absent.

I did not inspect any of them.

This qualified as personal growth only if standards had collapsed.

My body was ordinary. Right hand fine. Shoulders fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Both grips normal. Left tip normal.

The room needed sweeping.

Not dramatically.

There was no visible layer of filth proving moral decline. Just grit near the door, two onion skins that had escaped supper, thread ends near Lyssa's work chair, and the fine gray dust that Carrow generated from apparently nothing.

I swept.

The thread ends went into the rubbish.

I hesitated over one because it was dark reddish-brown.

Then I looked at myself holding a piece of rubbish between two fingers and dropped it with the others.

Healthy.

I had just finished when somebody knocked.

Not theatre knock.

Not Hessa's precise knock.

Not the hard two-beat knock used by boys carrying messages from people who expected answers.

Three quick taps, a pause, then one more.

I opened the door.

A woman stood outside holding a wooden bowl against one hip.

I knew her face.

This was becoming a dangerous category.

She lived somewhere close. I had passed her on the stairs or near the pump enough times that we had reached the stage of mutual recognition without information.
